name: Chitai Golu Devta Temple
deity: Golu Devta (Goljyu Maharaj), revered as an incarnation of Bhairava
significance: The best-known shrine of Golu Devta, a regional god of justice worshipped throughout Kumaon and Garhwal and treated as a form of Bhairava. It stands on the ridge at Chitai outside Almora and draws petitioners who bring their grievances to the deity.
story: A prince born to King Halrai was cast into the Gori river by jealous co-queens and rescued by a fisherman; he later returned to expose the injustice and was deified as the god of justice.

name: Kainchi Dham
significance: An ashram and temple complex in the Kumaon hills established by the saint Neem Karoli Baba in 1964 on land donated by a local devotee. It draws large numbers of Indian and Western visitors and is widely known through the saint's association with figures in the technology industry.

name: Surkanda Devi Temple
style: Himalayan stone shikhara topped by a trident
significance: A Shakta pitha perched at about 2,756 m above Kaddukhal near Dhanaulti in the Garhwal Himalaya. It is counted among the seats where a part of the goddess Sati is believed to have fallen, and is reached by a steep walk from the road head.
story: After Sati immolated herself and Shiva carried her body in grief, Vishnu dismembered it and her head is said to have fallen on this peak.

name: Adi Badri
dynasty: Late Gupta; foundation traditionally attributed to Adi Shankara
significance: A cluster of small stone shrines at Adibadri in Chamoli district, some 17 km beyond Karnaprayag, counted among the Sapta Badri. Assigned to the late Gupta period, it gave pilgrims a place to worship Vishnu when the high shrine at Badrinath was shut by snow.

name: Har Ki Pauri
dynasty: Vikramaditya (traditional); later British-era and modern expansion
significance: The principal bathing ghat of Haridwar, at the point where the Ganga leaves the mountains for the plains. It is the ritual centre of the city's Kumbh Mela and of the daily evening Ganga aarti, and tradition credits its construction to King Vikramaditya.
story: The pool here, Brahmakund, is said to be where Garuda let fall drops of the nectar of immortality.

name: Mansa Devi Temple
significance: A hilltop shrine on Bilwa Parvat in the Sivalik range above Haridwar, counted among the town's Panch Tirth and regarded as a Siddh Peeth where wishes are granted. It is reached by a cable car or a footpath from the city.
story: Folklore holds that Mansa, born of Shiva's mind, was raised as an ordinary girl and won divine power through austerity.

name: Chandi Devi Temple
dynasty: Suchat Singh of Kashmir; image attributed to Adi Shankara
significance: A Siddh Peetha on Neel Parvat across the Ganga from Haridwar. The present building was raised in 1929 by Suchat Singh of Kashmir, while the principal image is traditionally said to have been installed by Adi Shankara in the 8th century.
story: The goddess Chandi is said to have rested on this hill after killing the demon kings Shumbha and Nishumbha.

name: Vishnuprayag
significance: The confluence of the Alaknanda and the Dhauliganga, and the first of the five Panch Prayag confluences on the Alaknanda. A Vishnu shrine stands beside the meeting of the rivers on the road to Badrinath.
story: The place is named for a belief that the sage Narada meditated here and Vishnu appeared before him.

name: Nandaprayag
deity: Sacred confluence of the Alaknanda and Nandakini
significance: The second of the Panch Prayag, where the Nandakini joins the Alaknanda in Chamoli district. The town was historically the capital of the Yadu kingdom and is a halt on the Badrinath pilgrim road.

name: Karnaprayag
significance: One of the Panch Prayag, at the confluence of the Alaknanda and the Pindar in Chamoli district. A temple of the goddess Uma stands at the meeting of the rivers.
story: Karna of the Mahabharata is believed to have worshipped the sun god at this confluence.

name: Rudraprayag
significance: One of the Panch Prayag, where the Mandakini flowing down from Kedarnath meets the Alaknanda. The Rudranath temple, dedicated to Shiva in his Rudra aspect, stands at the confluence.
story: The sage Narada is said to have meditated at the Narad Shila here to learn music from Shiva.

name: Devprayag
style: Massive stone masonry, pyramidal form with a white cupola
significance: The last of the Panch Prayag, where the Alaknanda and the Bhagirathi join and the river continues as the Ganges. Above the confluence stands the Raghunathji temple, a stone shrine of pyramidal form capped by a white cupola.

name: Naimisharanya
significance: A sacred forest tract at Nimsar in Sitapur district, named repeatedly in the Puranas and in both epics. Tradition holds that the Puranas were first recited here to an assembly of sages, and the site remains an active pilgrimage centre.
story: The Varaha Purana explains the name by saying that a host of daityas was destroyed here within a single nimisha, an instant.

name: Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple
deity: Hanuman (as Sankat Mochan, remover of troubles)
significance: Varanasi's foremost Hanuman temple, traditionally founded by the poet-saint Tulsidas in the early 16th century. It is closely tied to the composition of the Ramcharitmanas and remains one of the busiest shrines in the city.
story: The temple is said to stand on the exact spot where Tulsidas had a vision of Hanuman.

name: Durga Mandir (Durga Kund Temple)
significance: An 18th-century Durga temple beside the Durga Kund tank in Varanasi, built at the expense of the Bengali queen Rani Bhabani of Natore. Its red-and-ochre exterior and adjoining stepped tank make it one of the city's most recognisable shrines.
story: The temple is said to commemorate Durga appearing on her lion to help the Kashi Naresh defeat invading kings, after which she promised to guard Varanasi.

name: Tulsi Manas Mandir
style: White marble, with the Ramcharitmanas engraved on the walls
significance: A white marble temple built in 1964 by the Sureka family at the place where Tulsidas is believed to have composed the Ramcharitmanas. Verses and scenes from that work are carved across its interior walls.

name: Shri Radha Rani Temple (Ladli Ji)
deity: Radha and Krishna, worshipped together as Shri Laadli Lal
dynasty: Bir Singh Deo; earlier structure associated with Narayan Bhatt and Raja Todar Mal
style: Rajput, in red sandstone with carved arches and domes
significance: The hill temple of Radha at Barsana, built in red sandstone in 1675 and the focus of the town's Radhashtami and Lathmar Holi festivals. It is among the principal Braj pilgrimage sites.
story: Radha's father Vrishbhanu is said to have made his home on the Bhanugarh hill at Barsana after leaving Kamsa's Mathura.

name: Prem Mandir
significance: A large modern marble temple complex at Vrindavan, begun in 2001 and inaugurated in 2012 at the initiative of Jagadguru Kripalu Maharaj. Its 22-hectare grounds hold life-size tableaux of Krishna's pastimes and a pillar-free satsang hall.

name: Radha Vallabh Temple
significance: The principal seat of the Radha Vallabh Sampradaya in Vrindavan, built in 1585 by Sundardas Bhatnagar under the guidance of Hith Harivansh Mahaprabhu with support from Akbar's court. It is among the oldest surviving temples of the town.
story: The image is said never to have been carved but to have been given directly by Shiva to a devotee named Atmadev.

name: Krishna Balaram Mandir (ISKCON Vrindavan)
significance: One of the largest ISKCON temples in the world, opened at Raman Reti in Vrindavan in 1975 under A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada. Its central altar holds Krishna and Balarama, and a marble samadhi shrine to the founder stands in the compound.

name: Dwarkadhish Temple
dynasty: Gwalior State (Scindia); built by Seth Gokul Das Parikh
significance: A Pushtimarg temple of 1814 in the old city of Mathura, raised by the Gwalior treasurer Seth Gokul Das Parikh with the approval of Daulatrao Scindia. It is among the busiest shrines in the town.

name: Vishram Ghat
significance: The central bathing ghat on the Yamuna at Mathura, where the town's circumambulation pilgrimage begins and ends. Its steps and shrines were built up over centuries by noble and royal patrons.
story: Krishna is said to have rested here after killing Kamsa, which gives the ghat its name, the ghat of rest.

name: Daan-Ghati Temple
significance: The main temple of Govardhan town, standing at the Daan Ghati pass through Govardhan Hill. It is a principal halt on the Govardhan parikrama and the focus of the town's Govardhan Puja observances.
story: Krishna is said to have raised Govardhan Hill on his little finger here to shelter the cowherds from Indra's storm.

name: Shakumbhari Devi Temple
significance: A Siddhpeeth in the Shivalik foothills of Behat tehsil, Saharanpur district, dedicated to the goddess of vegetation and nourishment. It is one of the larger pilgrimage centres of northern Uttar Pradesh.
story: When the demon Durgamasura brought a hundred-year famine, Adi Shakti appeared as Shakumbhari, whose tears fell as rain and who fed the world with food produced by her own power.

name: Chintpurni Temple
significance: A hill shrine about 40 km north of Una in Himachal Pradesh, counted among the 51 Shakta pithas and one of the busiest pilgrimage sites in the state. Its founding is credited to the brahmin Mai Das roughly twelve generations ago.
story: Sati's consciousness is said to have fallen here when Vishnu severed her burning body into fifty-one parts.

name: Naina Devi Temple
significance: A hilltop Shakta pitha in Bilaspur district overlooking the Govind Sagar reservoir, reached by road and by cable car. It is revered as the place where the right eye of the goddess Sati fell.
story: A Gurjar boy is said to have found the site when his white cow shed her milk over a stone, and the goddess then revealed herself to him in a dream, prompting Raja Bir Chand to build the temple.

name: Bajreshwari Mata Temple (Brajeshwari Devi)
deity: Durga as Vajreshwari, goddess of the thunderbolt
dynasty: Modern reconstruction; earlier shrine ascribed in legend to the Pandavas
significance: A Shakta pitha at Kangra town, counted among the fifty-one seats of the goddess and one of the most visited temples of Himachal Pradesh. The present building replaced the shrine destroyed by the 1905 Kangra earthquake.
story: The left breast of Sati is said to have fallen here when Vishnu divided her body into fifty-one parts.

name: Baijnath Temple
deity: Shiva as Vaidyanath, lord of physicians
dynasty: Built by the merchants Ahuka and Manyuka in the reign of Jaya Chandra; renovated under Sansar Chand
significance: A stone Nagara-style Shiva temple of 1204 CE at Baijnath in Kangra, protected by the Archaeological Survey of India. It came through the 1905 Kangra earthquake with little damage and remains in worship.
story: Ravana is said to have set down a Shiva lingam here while carrying it to Lanka, and out of respect for his devotion the town does not celebrate Dussehra.
